1.meaning: It has distracted you (plural) and pulled you away — kept you so busy and preoccupied that you neglected what truly matters. The verb carries the sense of being amused, diverted, and engrossed in something to the point of forgetting something more important.

parts.en: it distracted / diverted (caused to be heedless)

1.grammar: This is a past-tense verb (form IV, the causative 'al-hā', literally 'to cause to be diverted'). It is third-person masculine singular — 'it has distracted' — and its grammatical subject is the noun that follows ('the rivalry'). The attached ending '-kum' is the object 'you all' (plural); its vowel appears here as '-kumu' (an extra 'u') purely to ease pronunciation before the next word beginning with 'al-'. So the whole word means 'it has distracted you all'.
1.root: ل-ه-و (l-h-w) — distraction, diversion, amusement, heedless play

2.meaning: The frantic rivalry to pile up more and more — competing and boasting over wealth, children, status and worldly gains, each party trying to outdo the other in sheer quantity. The form of the word stresses a back-and-forth, mutual contest in seeking increase.

parts.en: mutual rivalry to amass / outdo one another in increase
(nominative ending: marks it as the subject)

2.grammar: This is a verbal noun on the form 'tafāʿul' (takāthur), a pattern that signals reciprocal, mutual action — many people competing against each other to have more. It carries the definite article 'al-' ('the'). The final '-u' ending is nominative, which marks it as the doer/subject of the verb in word 1: it is 'the rivalry' that has done the distracting. (The small mark after it is a recitation pause sign, not part of the word.)
2.root: ك-ث-ر (k-th-r) — abundance, multitude, being or becoming much/many

1.meaning: A connecting particle meaning 'until' or 'up to the point that.' It marks the end-limit of the preceding action: the heedless rivalry of verse 1 keeps going right up until the moment described next. It carries the sense of 'so much so that, eventually...'

parts.en: until / up to the point that

1.grammar: A particle of limit (ghāya) — it sets the boundary at which the previous action stops. Here it introduces a past-tense verb, giving the force 'until at last you...'. Particles like this do not change for case, tense, or person; the form is fixed.

2.meaning: 'You visited' / 'you came to' — but used here with grim irony for reaching and entering the graves, i.e. dying and being buried. The imagery of a 'visit' underlines that worldly life and even the grave are temporary stops, not the final destination.
2.grammar: A past-tense (perfect) verb. The attached ending -tum is the subject 'you all' (plural) — the doers of the action, set in the past ('you visited'). The rāʾ carries a sukūn (no vowel), shown by the apostrophe in zur'tumu. The final vowel is lengthened to -tumu here only to ease pronunciation before the next word beginning with 'al-'; the core ending is -tum.
2.root: ز-و-ر (z-w-r) — to visit, to call upon

3.meaning: 'The graves' / the burial places — the plural of a single grave, picturing whole cemeteries. It stands for death itself: people keep competing for more until they are carried off to the graveyard.
3.grammar: A definite noun ('the graves'), plural. It is the object of the verb 'visited' (you visited what? — the graves), so it is in the accusative (object) case. Its ending is the ordinary accusative -a, which is the standard accusative marker for every Arabic noun. Separately, this word is a diptote of the mafāʿil (broken-plural) pattern: such words refuse tanwīn, and in the genitive they take -a instead of the usual genitive -i — but that diptote feature does not affect the ending here, since the accusative is -a in any case.

1.meaning: A sharp word of rebuke and restraint, like saying 'No indeed!', 'Stop!', or 'Not at all!'. It cuts off the heedless attitude described in the previous verses, warning the listener away from being deceived by worldly rivalry. It can also carry the sense of 'Truly, indeed' as a solemn alert about what is coming.
1.grammar: A particle of rebuke and deterrence (it does not change form). It does not take a case ending; the final -ā is simply part of the fixed word. Its job is to halt the listener and brace them for the warning that follows.

2.meaning: A particle placed before a present-tense verb to push its meaning into the future, like the English 'will' or 'shall'. It often signals a more distant or emphatic future than the shorter particle sa-, here lending a tone of looming certainty: 'you are surely going to...'.
2.grammar: A future-tense particle (it does not inflect and takes no case ending). It attaches in meaning to the verb after it, turning 'you know' into 'you will/shall come to know'. The fixed final -a is part of the word, not a case marker.

3.meaning: 'You (all) will come to know' — you will realize, recognize, and find out for certain. The plural address speaks to all the heedless people at once, promising that the truth they now ignore will become undeniable knowledge to them.
3.grammar: A present/future verb (form I, 'to know'). The ta- prefix marks a 'you' subject; the stem ʿlamu carries the three root letters ʿ-l-m; the -ūna ending makes it masculine plural ('you all') and is the marker of the indicative mood (the verb is left in its full, unaltered state because nothing here cuts it short). Together with sawfa before it, the meaning is 'you all will surely know'.

1.meaning: A connective particle meaning 'then' or 'again'. Here it does not signal a time-gap so much as it adds a second, separate warning on top of the first one in the previous ayah, giving a sense of 'and once more...' — a deliberate, emphatic repetition.
1.grammar: An indeclinable connective particle (it never changes its ending). Unlike the simpler 'and', it adds something further in sequence or rank; placed before a repeated warning it reinforces it, conveying 'then yet again'.

2.meaning: A sharp word of rebuke and restraint, roughly 'No indeed!' or 'Stop!'. It rejects the heedless attitude described earlier and braces the listener for the warning that follows; it is far stronger than an ordinary 'no'.
2.grammar: An indeclinable particle of deterrence and rebuke (its ending never changes). It functions as a stern interjection that checks the hearer and affirms the truth of what comes next, like saying 'Absolutely not — beware!'

3.meaning: A particle that places the action firmly in the future — 'shall' or 'will'. It points to something certain that has not happened yet, here the coming realisation, and its length adds a note of 'in time, eventually'.
3.grammar: An indeclinable future particle (no changeable ending). Prefixed in sense to the verb that follows, it turns 'you know' into 'you will come to know', signalling a future event that is sure to occur.

4.meaning: 'You will come to know' — addressed to a group. It warns that the people lost in worldly rivalry will, in time, gain full knowledge of the truth and its consequences, knowledge they are presently ignoring.

parts.en: you know / come to know (2nd person, from the ta- prefix)

4.grammar: A present/future-tense (imperfect) verb. The ta- prefix encodes the second person ('you'); the -ūna ending encodes a masculine plural subject and keeps the verb in its base (indicative / رفع) mood. Together they give 'you (all) know'. With sawfa before it, the sense is future: 'you all shall come to know'.

1.meaning: A sharp word of rebuke and restraint meaning roughly 'No indeed!' or 'Stop!' It checks the heedless person mid-course, rejecting the obsession with worldly competition described in the previous verses and bracing the listener for the solemn warning that follows.
1.grammar: This is an indeclinable particle of deterrence and rebuttal, so it never changes its ending. It does not take a case or tense; it functions as a stand-alone exclamation that negates and rebukes at once, like saying 'Absolutely not!' before a warning.

2.meaning: A conditional particle introducing an unreal or unfulfilled condition: 'if (only)'. It signals that the condition is contrary to fact, the people in fact do NOT truly know, and it implies an unstated consequence ('...you would never behave as you do').
2.grammar: This is an indeclinable particle, so it has no case ending. It specifically sets up a hypothetical that is contrary to fact (unlike 'in', the particle for open/real conditions), which is why the verse leaves the result unspoken for emphasis: the answer is too dreadful to state.

3.meaning: 'You (all) know / truly come to have certain knowledge.' It describes the act of really knowing and being aware, here addressed to a group and tied to the 'if only' before it.
3.grammar: A present/imperfect verb. The ta- prefix plus the -ūna ending together mark 'you all' (second person, masculine plural), and the -ūna ending also shows the verb is in its base (indicative) state. After the particle 'law' the present tense keeps its present, ongoing force: it states a condition unfulfilled right now — 'if you [really, here and now] knew' — not a completed past event. The point is that the people's heedlessness is current and continuing.

4.meaning: 'Knowledge' in the sense of sure, real awareness. Paired with the next word it forms the phrase 'the knowledge of certainty' — knowing something so firmly that no doubt remains.
4.grammar: A noun functioning as a cognate (absolute) object of the verb 'you know' — 'you know a knowing' — and this cognate-object role is what puts it in the accusative case, shown by its -a ending; it intensifies the verb ('know with a real knowing'). Separately, it is the first term of a possessive pairing (iḍāfa) with the following word: that structural pairing, not the accusative vowel, is what links it to 'certainty' and requires the next word to be genitive ('knowledge OF...').

5.meaning: 'Certainty' — absolute, doubt-free conviction. 'Knowledge of al-yaqin' means the kind of sure knowing that would, if people possessed it now, transform how they live, since they would grasp the reality of death and the Hereafter beyond all doubt.
5.grammar: A noun with the attached 'al-' meaning 'the'. Its final -i ending is the genitive case, because it is the second term (muḍāf ilayhi) of the possessive pairing with the preceding word, forming 'the knowledge OF certainty.' Being that second term in the iḍāfa is exactly what makes it genitive.

1.meaning: A solemn, emphatic divine promise: "you will most certainly see it." This is not an ordinary statement but a doubly-stressed assurance — Allah swears that the people will, beyond any doubt, behold the Fire with their own eyes.

parts.en: surely / by all means (oath of emphasis)
you all (waw of plurality — masculine plural subject)

1.grammar: Two emphasizers wrap a single verb. The opening la- is the lam of oath, as if to say "I swear you will…"; the closing -nna is the heavy emphatic ending (nun al-tawkid) meaning "most certainly." The ta- prefix marks the subject as "you," and the waw (waw al-jamaa) marks it as masculine plural ("you all"). Note the normal form is tarawna ("you all see"); when the heavy emphatic -nna is attached, the plural's own final nun (nun al-jam) drops, and the waw remains carrying a damma, giving tarawunna. The whole word is in the energetic mood, used for binding promises and threats.
1.root: ر-أ-ي (r-ʾ-y) — to see, to perceive with the eye

2.meaning: The blazing Hellfire — al-Jaheem, one of the Qur'an's names for the Fire of the Hereafter, evoking something fiercely kindled and raging. Here it is the very thing the people are promised they will witness.
2.grammar: Al- is "the," marking it as the specific, well-known Fire. The crucial mark is the final -a (fatha): it is the accusative ending, which shows that al-Jaheema is the direct object — the thing being seen. So it answers "you will see WHAT?" — "the Hellfire." The word jaheem is an intensive form, conveying a fire that blazes and rages rather than a mere flame.
2.root: ج-ح-م (j-ḥ-m) — to blaze fiercely, to kindle into a raging fire

1.meaning: A connector meaning "then" or "thereafter." Unlike a simple "and," it signals a further, distinct stage — here it adds a second, heavier emphasis on top of verse 6, escalating the warning: not only will you see the Fire, but then you will see it again with absolute certainty.
1.grammar: An indeclinable connecting particle (it never changes its ending). It links two statements while marking sequence and a step up in intensity, ordering one event or assertion after another rather than merely joining them.

2.meaning: "You will most certainly see it." A solemn, doubly emphasized promise that the people addressed will, with their own eyes, behold the blazing Fire. The "it" refers back to the Hellfire (al-jaḥīm) mentioned in the previous verse.
2.grammar: The prefixed لَ (la-) is the emphatic particle that answers an implied oath — "By Allah, you shall surely…" The verb is present/future tense, second-person masculine plural ("you all"), built on the root "to see." Its ending carries the heavy emphatic nūn (the doubled -nn-), which turns a plain "you will see" into an unbreakable "you will definitely see"; this nūn also displaces the normal plural -ūna ending, leaving the -u- before it, and it takes a fatḥa (-a) when an object pronoun follows — hence tarawunna before -hā. The final هَا (-hā) is an attached object pronoun, "it," pointing to the Fire.

3.meaning: "With the very eye of" — i.e. with direct eyesight. Paired with the next word it forms the expression "the eye of certainty" (ʿayn al-yaqīn): knowledge so sure it is like seeing a thing with your own eyes, the certainty of firsthand sight as opposed to mere report.
3.grammar: A noun in the accusative case, shown by the final -a. The accusative here works adverbially, describing the manner of seeing — "see it by way of the eye of…" It is also the first half of a possessive pair ("the eye OF certainty"), governing the genitive word that follows.

4.meaning: "Certainty" — firm, doubt-free conviction. As the second half of the phrase "the eye of certainty," it conveys the highest grade of sureness: truth confirmed by direct vision, leaving no possibility of doubt.
4.grammar: The prefix الۡ (al-) is the definite article, "the." The final -i is the genitive ending, produced because this word is the possessed second term of the pair "eye OF certainty" — the genitive case is what links it back to "eye" and expresses the "of" relationship.

1.meaning: A connector meaning 'then' or 'thereafter.' Unlike a simple 'and,' it signals a sequence with a sense of interval or rank — one thing following another after a gap. Here it moves the warning forward to a further, climactic stage: after seeing the Fire comes the questioning.
1.grammar: A connecting particle (conjunction). It is indeclinable — it never changes its ending — so the final -a is fixed and carries no case meaning. It orders events in succession with a pause: 'and then, after that.'

2.meaning: 'You will most certainly be questioned.' It is built as a passive — the focus is on the people being interrogated, not on who does the asking (Allah). The wording is doubly emphatic, conveying an unbreakable certainty: there is no escaping this accounting.
2.grammar: A present/future-tense passive verb, 2nd person masculine plural ('you all'). Two layers stack the emphasis: the prefixed la- ('surely') and the heavy emphatic nūn (-nna) at the end, which together turn it into a solemn oath-like promise ('you will absolutely be asked'). The tu- prefix with the vowel pattern marks it as passive ('are asked,' not 'ask'). The base stem is tus'alu; the masculine plural normally adds -ūna (tus'alūna), but before the heavy nūn that plural wāw (-ū) drops out and a short -u links the stem to the ending, giving tus'al + u + nna = tus'alunna. The plural sense is still carried by that ending.

3.meaning: 'On that Day' — meaning the Day of Resurrection and Judgement. It pins the questioning to that single, specific, momentous Day already in view.
3.grammar: A time-word, 'day,' fused with the particle idh ('then') to mean 'on that day.' The whole expression works as an adverb of time (when the questioning happens). Yawm itself carries the fatḥa (-a), its accusative/adverbial ending. The attached idh is the second term of the construct (the noun it is annexed to), so it takes the genitive; here that genitive shows up as tanwīn — idhin is idh + the -in ending (the kasra plus the 'n' sound called nunation). So the -i belongs to idh's genitive tanwīn, not to yawm.

4.meaning: 'About' or 'concerning' — it introduces the subject of the interrogation: what you will be asked about.
4.grammar: A preposition meaning 'about / concerning.' Its base form is ʿan (عَنْ). The final -i here is not a case ending but a connecting vowel: the resting nūn is given a kasra to glide smoothly into the 'al-' of the next word and avoid two unvoweled consonants clashing.

5.meaning: 'The blessings/pleasures' — the comforts and good things of this life: health, security, food, leisure, every favour Allah grants. The point is that these gifts carry responsibility, and one will be asked whether they were received with gratitude and used rightly.
5.grammar: A noun, 'the blessings/delights,' with the attached al- ('the'). The final -i ending is the genitive case, which is required because it follows the preposition ʿan ('about') — so it reads 'about the blessings.' (The 'l' of al- assimilates into the following 'n,' which is why it is pronounced an-naʿīm.)
